presets.name: EMC · epoxy + fused silica 50 vol%
presets.description: Semiconductor mould compound. Spherical silica with a log-normal size distribution governs the CTE and the thermal conductivity.

presets.name: Underfill · epoxy + SiO₂ 40 vol% (1 µm)
presets.description: Flip-chip underfill; the objective is CTE matching with the solder bumps.

presets.name: TIM · silicone + Al₂O₃ 50 vol% with interfacial resistance
presets.description: Thermal gap filler. The interfacial (Kapitza) resistance introduces a filler-size effect.

presets.name: TIM · epoxy + AlN 40 vol%
presets.description: High-conductivity epoxy composite. With the large filler contrast, the resin films and the contacts between particles govern k.

presets.name: Thermal sheet · silicone + h-BN platelets 25 vol% (in-plane aligned)
presets.description: Platelets lying in the xy plane produce very different in-plane and through-plane conductivities.

presets.name: Porous low-k film · SiO₂ + 30 % connected porosity
presets.description: Mesoporous silica low-k dielectric; permittivity, stiffness, thermal conductivity with rarefied gas in the nanopores, and the pore-entry size distribution.

presets.name: Sintered silver die attach · Ag + 15 % porosity
presets.description: Power-module die attach; reduction of thermal and electrical conductivity and stiffness by porosity.

presets.name: Conductive adhesive · epoxy + Ag flakes 20 vol%
presets.description: Oblate spheroids (thickness/diameter 0.15) aligned in plane; in-plane and through-plane percolation are compared.

presets.name: EMI shielding · epoxy + Ni rods 12 vol%
presets.description: Magnetic metal rods; electrical percolation and permeability determine the shielding effectiveness.

presets.name: Low-Dk substrate · PPE + hollow silica 30 vol%
presets.description: Hollow silica (0.3 µm shell) lowers Dk; the shell thickness sets the required resolution.

presets.name: Low CTE · epoxy + ZrW₂O₈ 40 vol%
presets.description: Negative-thermal-expansion filler lowering the composite CTE (conditions of the NTE study).

presets.name: High-k · epoxy + BaTiO₃ 30 vol%
presets.description: Embedded-capacitor dielectric. The ferroelectric filler contrast makes the inter-particle distance govern Dk and the local field enhancement.

presets.name: Porous ceramic · Al₂O₃ + 35 % porosity (vacuum chuck, filter)
presets.description: Porous chuck and filter ceramics: permeability, tortuosity, intrusion porosimetry, pore network, radiative extinction and thermal conductivity in one run.

presets.name: UPW filter membrane · PTFE + 70 % porosity (bubble point)
presets.description: Wet-process filter membrane: largest through-pore and isopropanol bubble point, flow resistance, tortuosity and pore network.

presets.name: Sintered gas filter · SUS316L + 40 % porosity
presets.description: Point-of-use gas filter: permeability, pore-entry size, bubble point, filtration efficiency, pore network and thermal conductivity of sintered stainless steel.

presets.name: Fibrous insulation · E-glass fibres 8 vol% in air
presets.description: Equipment insulation and acoustic lining: fibres lying in the xy plane; thermal conductivity, sound absorption (JCA) and radiative extinction.

presets.name: MUF · epoxy + silica 15 + 3 µm 55 vol% (flowability, thermal conductivity)
presets.description: Moulded underfill: effective viscosity, flow curve, maximum packing fraction, capillary filling of a 50 µm bump gap and filler settling before cure, and the thermal conductivity of the cured compound. Every input is backed in guide 32.1 ("Why these input values"): 55–70 vol% silica in encapsulants, the largest particle at most a third of the gap, a 70/30 bimodal blend; resin, wetting and rate values are representative and marked to be replaced by measurements. Replace the two silica phases with one 5 µm phase to see why the blend flows about twice as easily.

presets.name: MUF · from flow to the cured part (silica 15 + 3 µm 55 vol%, after shear flow)
presets.description: The MUF of the viscosity example, cured where its flow leaves it: the packing is sheared in the resin by particle dynamics to a strain of 10 (Domain → Particle arrangement → After shear flow), flow along x and its gradient through z - across the gap the compound fills. The viscosity, flow curve, filling time and settling come from the particle dynamics; thermal conductivity, CTE and modulus, Dk/Df and moisture uptake are solved on that one cured structure (60 µm, 240³ voxels). Computed with touching particles (5.10.2, the thermal conductivity on the finite volume): k 0.596 W/m·K through the gap (0.576 for the random packing it started from), CTE 16.5 ppm/K, E 15.0 GPa, Dk 3.84, Df 0.0068, 0.77 wt% moisture at saturation; the flow raised the close pairs of particles from 1.7 to 3.8 per sphere. The shear takes minutes on an NVIDIA GPU and about 17 minutes on 14 CPU cores; the solves need about 6 GB (the three conduction directions side by side). Since 5.12.0 the thermal conductivity is solved on the tetrahedral FEM by default, about 60 GB at 240³; Simulation → Solver settings → Thermal conductivity → Periodic finite volume on the voxels runs it as computed here.

form.name: MUF · cured after shear flow, silica 15 + 3 µm 55 vol%

presets.name: DOE · MUF Al₂O₃ 250 nm + BN platelet stacks 55 vol% (BN 5–50 % of the filler)
presets.description: A study, ready in the DOE tab: 55 vol% filler of 250 nm alumina spheres, 5 to 50 % of which (in steps of 5) is replaced by h-BN as stacks of 4 platelets (2 µm × 300 nm × 4 × 50 nm, rounded edges), lying in the plane of the part (thickness axis within 15° of z). The platelets conduct 300 W/m·K in their plane and 30 through it; through a stack the 4 layers and the 3 plate-plate contacts (1.2e-8 m²K/W) are in series, about 4.7 W/m·K. Filler-resin interface resistance 4.8e-8 and contact resistance 1.2e-8 m²K/W for both fillers. Thermal conductivity (x, y in the plane; z through it) and viscosity of every case (particle dynamics of the RVE's own particles, rigid multi-sphere stacks with the spheres - an NVIDIA GPU is recommended). Every case on one fixed grid, 4 µm at 25 nm voxels (160³). Single 50 nm platelets dispersed among the spheres cannot fill 55 vol% beyond about 5 % BN; as stacks the packing reaches the target size, and after the exact-shape repair the RVE holds 53.8 vol% at 25 % BN (13.2 vol% BN) and 51.4 vol% at 50 % (24.8 vol% BN, a share of 48 %) - each run reports the content it reached.

form.name: MUF · Al₂O₃ 250 nm + BN platelet stacks 55 vol%

doe.name: MUF · BN share of the filler 5–50 %

presets.name: Calibration · MUF Al₂O₃ 250 nm 55 vol%: interface and contact resistance from k = 0.54 W/m·K
presets.description: A calibration, ready in the Calibration tab: a moulded underfill of 250 nm alumina spheres at 55 vol% in the MUF epoxy. The measurement, 0.54 W/m·K (± 5 %), is reproducible: it is this RVE's own result on the FEM (0.537) for R_int = 1e-7 m²K/W - the phonon-mismatch (DMM) value of a perfect epoxy-alumina interface, 9.6e-8 - and R_c = 2e-7, so the answer can be checked. The unknowns are the filler-resin interfacial resistance R_int and the contact resistance R_c, in series with the resin film where two touching particles meet, each searched from 1e-10 to 1e-6 m²K/W. Computed on the tetrahedral FEM (70³ lattice of 25 nm, 4.8 million tetrahedra built once; 14 parameter sets, about 7 min on 18 threads): without resistance the compound conducts 1.23 W/m·K; R_int acts on every particle-resin surface and R_c only on the films, so this one measurement narrows R_int to 5.4e-8 - 3.6e-7 (estimate 1.4e-7) and leaves R_c open - it fixes the combination ln R_int + 0.26 ln R_c, on which the true pair lies. A second sample in which the contacts weigh differently, a lower content or another particle size, separates the two. Linking R_c = 2·R_int instead (one unknown) gives R_int = 9.9e-8 (95 % 7.6e-8 - 1.24e-7), with the factor 2 as an assumption; R_int alone, with contacts free of resistance, gives 2.4e-7, standing for the contacts as well (guide 30.9).

cal.name: MUF · Al₂O₃ 250 nm 55 vol% · R_int and R_c from k = 0.54

presets.name: EMC reliability · epoxy + silica 40 vol% (moisture, swelling, above Tg)
presets.description: Moisture diffusivity, saturated uptake, the uptake curve of a 0.5 mm part at 85 °C / 85 % RH and the hygroscopic swelling (CME), together with the CTE and modulus below and above the glass transition (α1 / α2) of a moulding compound (guide chapter 14). Computed with touching particles (the default): 1.125 wt% at saturation, α1 27.2 / α2 61 ppm/K, E 8.90 / 0.33 GPa. Above Tg the touching particles form a rigid skeleton; with a gap between particles of 2 voxels (Structure tab) α2 is 95.5 ppm/K and the hot modulus 0.126 GPa (guide 14.5).

presets.name: Highly filled · epoxy + silica 64 vol%, one size (at random close packing: grown in place)
presets.description: 64 vol% of equal silica spheres, at the random close packing of equal spheres (64.3 %, Farr-Groot). The packing stops just short of full size; the overlap Auto (Structure → Gap between particles) draws the spheres at their full size where they stand, because the rest is within 2 % of their size: touching neighbours then overlap by at most that much - the depth of roughness and squeezed-out resin between real particles - and the tetrahedral FEM separates them again at a face with a resin film. The RVE checks report the growth. Set 66 vol% to see a loading beyond the rule: no arrangement of equal spheres holds it without overlaps deeper than real particles have, so the structure is packed with less content and the run stops before the solves; a broader size distribution packs denser. Overlap → Voxel steps reaches 66 vol% with whole voxels of overlap, for comparison with versions up to 5.11.

presets.name: Thin film · polyimide + h-BN platelets 25 vol%, 15 µm
presets.description: A 15 µm film: x and y periodic, z the real thickness, every platelet inside the film. The platelets lie in the plane, so the in-plane thermal conductivity is about 2.3 times the through-plane value that a heat-spreading film is judged by (0.62 against 0.27 W/m·K; guide 6.5).

presets.name: Noise-suppression sheet · epoxy + Sendust flakes 25 vol% (permeability)
presets.description: Flat magnetic flakes lying in the plane of the sheet: the in-plane permeability is nearly four times the through-plane value (μr 7.04 against 1.86), because the flux crosses fewer resin gaps (guide chapter 10). Compare with spheres of the same content.

presets.name: Hybrid TIM · silicone + Al₂O₃ 10 µm + AlN 3 µm 55 vol% (blend, contacts)
presets.description: Two fillers of different size and material: the small AlN fills the gaps between the large Al₂O₃. Each filler has its own interfacial resistance, and the contact resistance between the two fillers is set separately (Structure tab). Particles may touch, as in a real gap filler; Fast quality keeps the run short - use Standard for values to report.

form.name: Hybrid TIM · Al₂O₃ 10 µm + AlN 3 µm

presets.name: Statistical RVE · TIM silicone + Al₂O₃ 50 vol%: small boxes until the mean settles
presets.description: An RVE too large to solve, replaced by small boxes: the gap filler is solved on a 60 µm box of 10 µm alumina (six diameters, below the Standard level's seven), again and again with a new random arrangement, until the 95 % confidence interval of the mean conductivity is within 2 % (at least 3, at most 40 realisations; Domain → Realisations → Until the mean settles). Kanit et al. (Int. J. Solids Struct. 40 (2003) 3647, doi:10.1016/S0020-7683(03)00143-4) showed that the mean over enough small volumes gives the effective property, provided the volume is not so small that it biases the mean. It settles within 2 % after 20 realisations (52 s on 18 threads). The RVE checks report the realisations used, their scatter and how many a ±1 % interval would need. A box of four diameters would scatter by 7.2 % and, worse, its mean lies 9 % low - biased; from six diameters on the means agree (guide 6.7). Run the compound once at a larger RVE to confirm.

form.name: Statistical RVE · TIM silicone + Al₂O₃ 50 vol%

presets.name: Heat spreader · Cu + diamond 50 vol% (400 µm, interface from a measurement)
presets.description: Cu/diamond for high-power, GaN and SiC devices. Wang et al. (Materials 18 (2025) 3882, doi:10.3390/ma18163882) hot-pressed 400 µm diamond (1717 W/m·K) at 50 vol% in Cu (385 W/m·K) with a 200 nm W coating and measured 640 W/m·K. On the tetrahedral FEM the RVE gives 640 W/m·K with an interface conductance of 10.6 MW/m²K (R_int 9.4e-8 m²K/W; touching diamonds 1.88e-7) - what the measurement says about the bonded interface. The 36-56 MW/m²K the paper estimates from effective-medium models give 767-794 W/m·K here, and a differential effective medium with the same inputs 775: the difference lies in the model's assumptions, not in the solve. The Calibration tab finds R_int from a measurement of your own.

presets.name: Power-module baseplate · Al-Si7Mg + SiC 63 vol% (AlSiC)
presets.description: AlSiC for IGBT and SiC module baseplates and lids: a CTE near the ceramic substrate with the conductivity of aluminium. Guo et al. (J. Univ. Sci. Technol. Beijing 36 (2014) 489-495, doi:10.13374/j.issn1001-053x.2014.04.011; tabulated in Lai et al., Micromachines 14 (2023) 1491, Table 2) measured pseudo-semi-solid thixoformed SiCp/Al at 63 vol%: 178 W/m·K and 8.21 ppm/K (56 vol%: 176 W/m·K, 9.25 ppm/K); this case gives 195 W/m·K (the tetrahedral FEM with the interface resistance on the true surfaces; 189 on the voxels) and 8.85 ppm/K (+10 %, +8 %). Bimodal SiC grit (60 + 20 µm, 3:1) as needed for such loadings, Al/SiC interface 1e-8 m²K/W, one fixed grid of 140³.

presets.name: mmWave substrate · PTFE + fused silica 60 wt%
presets.description: PTFE-silica laminate for 5G/6G antennas and RF front ends: silica brings the CTE of PTFE towards copper and keeps Dk near 3. Murali et al. (Composites Part A 40 (2009) 1179-1185, doi:10.1016/j.compositesa.2009.05.007) report Dk 2.9 and tan δ 0.0024 at X band for PTFE with 60 wt% micron silica; this case gives Dk 3.01. The loss of a real laminate comes from interfaces, moisture and voids that a mixture of perfect PTFE and silica does not have (here tan δ 0.0001): read the computed tan δ as the lower limit.

presets.name: PCB thermal vias · FR-4 with Cu-plated vias (0.3 mm, 1 mm pitch)
presets.description: The thermal pad of a QFN or power package sits on plated through-holes: 0.3 mm drill, 25 µm Cu plating, 1 mm pitch, 1.6 mm board. Each via is drawn as a copper rod with the cross-section of its plating (0.166 mm). Through the board the vias are parallel paths: k_z 8.95 W/m·K, the area-weighted mean of the drawn copper (2.16 %) and the FR-4 exactly - 31 times the laminate's 0.29; in the plane 0.85 (FR-4 0.81). That equality is a check of the solver against the exact solution for straight vias, not a measurement: a real board adds the pads and copper planes that spread the heat. A thin-film domain of the board thickness, so that the vias span it; change the content (the pitch) or the rod diameter (the plating) for the trade-off.

presets.name: Die-attach solder · SAC305 with 15 % voids
presets.description: X-ray inspection limits voiding in solder die attach to a few to 25 %. The voids are insulating spheres: this case gives 76.9 % of the dense conductivity at 15 %, below 2(1 - φ)/(2 + φ) = 79.1 %, Maxwell's upper bound for insulating spheres (a consistency check, not a measurement; a real joint adds the shape and place of its voids); the thermal resistance of the joint rises by the inverse. Vary the void content in the DOE tab for the resistance-voiding curve.

presets.name: Package-level power inductor · epoxy + carbonyl iron 54 vol%
presets.description: Magnetic core of a planar inductor for package-level power delivery. Sugawa et al. (IEEE Trans. Magn. 49 (2013) 4172-4175, doi:10.1109/TMAG.2013.2250925) report μr 7.5 for a screen-printed 54 vol% carbonyl-iron/epoxy core; spheres of iron (μr 50) in this case, touching where they meet, give 5.97. The resin gaps between the particles, not the iron, set the permeability: a printed paste has particle chains and agglomerates along which the flux crosses fewer gaps - try a higher content, flake-like particles or permitted overlap to see how fast μr rises.

presets.name: EMC · compression test (epoxy + silica 50 vol%)
presets.description: A compression test of a moulding compound as a universal testing machine runs it: a specimen 10 mm long with 10 mm² loaded to 100 MPa along z, sides free, and a matrix strength of 120 MPa entered as an input. The load runs through the effective stiffness of the RVE (elasticity is computed with it) and one more FANS solve gives the stress fields (guide 12.8). Computed on 70³ voxels of 0.5 µm (5 µm silica, 14 s on 18 threads): apparent modulus 14.29 GPa (Hill E 14.08 GPa), 1000 N for a shortening of 70.0 µm, Poisson's ratio 0.234 / 0.239; the most stressed 0.1 % of the epoxy reaches 120 MPa at 1033 N (103 MPa applied), the estimated onset of yielding between the particles. Linear elastic: tension gives the same line with the opposite sign.

presets.name: Compression · closed mould: epoxy + silica 30 vol% with 10 % voids, sides held
presets.description: A compound with trapped voids pressed in a closed mould: the RVE is shortened by 8 % along z with x and y held, so the volume lost must come from the voids. They close while the resin (1 Pa·s) flows around the rigid silica - three-dimensional creeping flow on the voxels, the voids a compressible gas, material markers for the resin (guide 5.5). Computed on 70³ voxels of 0.5 µm (206 s): voids 10.0 → 2.25 vol% (2.15 from the volume lost alone), the resin 60.0 → 65.0 % of the box, axial stress 70 Pa at 1 1/s, and k_z of the pressed part 0.369 W/m·K. Result Viewer → Compression replays the voids shrinking step by step in 3D.

form.name: Compression · closed mould: epoxy + silica 30 vol% with 10 % voids, sides held

presets.name: Compression · two resins side by side, sides free (resin + silica 40 vol% beside a neat resin)
presets.description: A neat resin beside a resin filled with 40 vol% silica, each in one half of the box along x, compressed by 30 % along z with the sides free. Both resins flow at 1 Pa·s; the rigid particles stiffen the filled half, so the neat half spreads more (guide 5.5). Computed on 70³ voxels of 0.5 µm (109 s): the box goes from 35³ µm to 43.5 × 40.5 × 24.5 µm, the neat half strains +0.237 along x and the filled half +0.188, and the resin between the particles takes -0.564 along z where its half as a whole takes -0.354. Axial stress 58 Pa at 1 1/s; k_z after the compression 0.333 W/m·K. Each resin keeps its volume share (0.500 → 0.502, 0.300 → 0.299).

form.name: Compression · two resins side by side, sides free (resin + silica 40 vol% beside a neat resin)

presets.name: Cure–flow · MUF pressed at 175 °C while it cures (silica 40 vol%, 1 %/s closing)
presets.description: A moulded underfill pressed at 1 %/s (a strain rate of 0.01 1/s) in a mould at 175 °C while its epoxy cures: Kamal-Sourour kinetics of an EMC from DSC (E1 67.91 / E2 67.34 kJ/mol, log A1 5.65 / A2 6.48, m 1.09, n 1.06; Franieck et al., Polymers 13 (2021) 1734, doi:10.3390/polym13111734) and the Castro-Macosko viscosity rising to the gel point (α_g 0.71, A -0.18, B 4.22; measured on a neat epoxy, not an EMC: Romberg et al., ACS Appl. Polym. Mater. 6 (2024), doi:10.1021/acsapm.4c00607). The mould asks for 55 %. Computed on 70³ voxels of 0.5 µm (230 s, 20 steps): the axial stress rises from 0.95 Pa (α 0) to 14 Pa at 38 % (α 0.47, 48 s), 114 Pa at 44 % (α 0.59, 58 s) and 2847 Pa at 47.8 % (α 0.67, 65 s); the compound gels at 69.2 s with the mould closed by 49.9 %. The RVE stays within 0.66 K of the mould (heat of reaction 177 J/g of resin, exchange time 0.32 s for a 1 mm part). A faster closing or a cooler mould lets it close before the gel point (guide 5.5).

form.name: Cure–flow · MUF pressed at 175 °C while it cures (silica 40 vol%, 1 %/s closing)

presets.name: Thermal stress and warpage · MUF 300 µm on a Si die in operation (die 125 °C, top 95 °C)
presets.description: A 300 µm moulded underfill (silica 8 µm, 50 vol%) on a 300 µm Si die in operation: the die side at 125 °C, the top at 95 °C, stress-free at the cure temperature of 175 °C (guide 12.9). Heat flows through the film with the conductivities of the thermal analysis; every voxel takes the thermal strain of its own temperature; classical laminate theory releases the film bonded to the die. Computed on 70 × 70 × 375 voxels of 0.8 µm (168 s): 51.4 kW/m² through the film (k_z 0.514 W/m·K), κ -1.03 1/m, warpage -12.89 µm over 10 mm (edges up; -11.97 µm at the uniform mean temperature, so the gradient adds -0.92 µm), the die at -36.9 MPa on its top face and +26.5 MPa at its bottom; in the epoxy the largest principal stress reaches 27.2 MPa and the peeling stress 25.9 MPa (99.9th percentiles), in the silica the von Mises stress 160 MPa. Elastic: no relaxation, no cure shrinkage.

form.name: Thermal stress and warpage · MUF 300 µm on a Si die in operation (die 125 °C, top 95 °C)

presets.name: Joule heating · Ag-filled adhesive joint 25 µm, current up to thermal runaway
presets.description: A silver-filled conductive adhesive joint 25 µm thick (5 µm Ag spheres, 45 vol%, touching the electrodes: no matrix skin) carrying a rising current density. The silver's resistance rises with temperature (TCR 0.0038 1/K, from the resistivity of Ag at 293 and 400 K in Matula, J. Phys. Chem. Ref. Data 8 (1979) 1147, doi:10.1063/1.555614), and the joint's path to ambient is a thermal resistance of 1e-4 K·m²/W (guide 8.8). Computed on 70 × 70 × 50 voxels of 0.5 µm (81 s): 0.95 MS/m through the joint at 5e7 A/m² (31.6 °C); 2.5e8 A/m² settles at 426 °C with the conductivity fallen to 0.39 MS/m, the film itself only 1.7 K above its faces - the path to ambient sets the temperature; at 3e8 A/m² the steady state lies above 1000 °C (1697 °C extrapolated) and the sweep stops. As one resistor the joint has a TCR of 0.0038 1/K and 25 µΩ·mm² at 20 °C, so a set current runs away above J ≈ 1/√(TCR·R20·R_th) = 3.2e8 A/m². Touching particles conduct across whole voxel faces (no electrical contact resistance): the conductivity is that of ideal contacts.

form.name: Joule heating · Ag-filled adhesive joint 25 µm, current up to thermal runaway

presets.name: Short glass fibres · epoxy + 12 vol% with diameter and length distributed independently
presets.description: Chopped or milled glass fibres: the diameter (normal, 6 ± 0.6 µm) and the length (log-normal, 36 ± 12 µm) each have a distribution of their own, so short thick and long thin fibres both occur. Thermal conductivity in and through the plane; Grain analysis sets the diameters, lengths and aspect ratios the structure holds against the input, and particles.csv lists every fibre.

presets.name: Alumina flakes · epoxy + 20 vol% triaxial flakes (three axes, c/a distributed)
presets.description: Platelets that are not round: the axes 2a = d (log-normal, 12 ± 3 µm), 2b = 0.6 d and the thickness 2c = c/a · d with c/a normal 0.25 ± 0.05 of its own, lying in the xy plane. Thermal conductivity in and through the plane; Grain analysis reports every axis and both aspect ratios against the input.

presets.name: Crushed silica · epoxy + 40 vol% irregular grains sized by their volume-equivalent diameter
presets.description: Angular fused silica as a laser-diffraction report gives it: the size entered (log-normal, mean 8 ± 3 µm) is the diameter of the sphere of the same volume, and every irregular grain is scaled to it. Thermal conductivity and CTE; Grain analysis reports the volume-equivalent diameter (as entered) and the circumscribed diameter of the grains against the input.

presets.name: Structure from a TIFF · a grey CT-like stack of an EMC (epoxy, silica, voids), split by thresholds
presets.description: An 8-bit image of 64 × 64 × 64 voxels of 1 µm shipped with MPSim (emc_ct_example.tif: voids dark, epoxy mid-grey, silica bright, with blur and noise, as a scan looks before segmentation). Three grey-value ranges from automatic (Otsu) thresholds become the voids, the epoxy matrix and the silica; thermal conductivity and Grain analysis (its particles, touching ones separated) run on the image as on a generated RVE. Your own image: Structure tab, Image (TIFF), Load TIFF.

presets.name: Viscosity from a TIFF · a scan-like stack of an uncured compound, touching silica spheres in resin
presets.description: An 8-bit image of 96 × 96 × 96 voxels of 0.5 µm shipped with MPSim (emc_visc_example.tif: resin mid-grey, fused silica bright, blurred and noisy as a scan), made from 90 touching spheres of mean diameter 9.93 µm (CV 0.25) at 50 vol%. A threshold splits resin and silica; the viscosity analysis separates the touching particles (90 found, mean 9.91 µm) and the particle dynamics shears them from where they are in the image, as spheres of their volume-equivalent sizes, with the MUF resin's flow curve; Grain analysis reports the same particles and writes them as particles.csv. Your own image: Structure tab, Image (TIFF), Load TIFF.

presets.name: Viscosity from a particle list · particles.csv of the same 90 silica spheres, drawn again without generating
presets.description: The particle file MPSim writes beside every run (particles.csv with particles_README.txt), shipped for the 90 touching fused-silica spheres (mean 9.93 µm, 50 vol%) the image of 'Viscosity from a TIFF' was made from. Structure - List (CSV) draws them on 96³ voxels of 0.5 µm as they were generated, without packing them again; the particle dynamics shears them from where they are. Your own run: Result Viewer - Grain analysis or the Export ribbon - Use as the structure, or Structure tab, List (CSV), Load CSV.

form.name: Uncured compound from a particle list

presets.name: FEM · alumina + BN compound on a tetrahedral mesh fitted to the particles
presets.description: The conduction solved by finite elements on a tetrahedral mesh fitted to the particles (Simulation → Solver settings → Thermal conductivity, the default since 5.12.0, and Other conduction properties for the permittivity), with the finite volume on the voxels beside it ('Also solve with the other method'). Alumina spheres (4 µm, log-normal) 45 vol% with BN platelets (3 × 3 × 0.6 µm) 5 vol% in epoxy, 16 µm RVE, 64³ voxels of 0.25 µm; thermal conductivity and permittivity along z (k 30 / 60 / 0.2 W/m·K, library values). Result (about 1 min): the mesh holds 2.89 million tetrahedra; 8,770 lattice edges run from one particle straight into another through a film of resin thinner than a voxel (median 0.12 µm), carried as interface elements, and 137 pairs that the packing left overlapping by less than a voxel are met as touching particles (Overlapping particles → Separated, the default since 5.12.0). k_z 1.57 W/m·K by the FEM against 4.13 W/m·K by the finite volume; ε_r 6.02 against 6.00. With the overlaps merged into necks, as up to 5.11, k_z is 2.49. The two differ where the contrast is high and the particles are close: on the voxels two particles conduct into each other wherever two of their voxels touch, on the fitted mesh they are the exact shapes with the resin films between them. The same particles drawn on finer and finer grids (guide 7.2): the finite volume 4.69 → 3.64 W/m·K from 32³ to 128³ and still falling, the FEM 1.66 → 1.55. The permittivity, of low contrast, agrees within 1 %. Which value fits a material depends on its contacts: fillers wetted by the resin are nearer the FEM, fillers pressed or sintered into each other nearer the finite volume (or the finite volume with a contact resistance calibrated on a measurement). Method: conformal decomposition finite elements (D. R. Noble, E. P. Newren, J. B. Lechman, Int. J. Numer. Meth. Fluids 63 (2010) 725, doi:10.1002/fld.2095); films as thin-gap conduction (G. K. Batchelor, R. W. O'Brien, Proc. R. Soc. Lond. A 355 (1977) 313, doi:10.1098/rspa.1977.0100); the same values as FEniCSx on the same mesh (self-test).

form.name: TIM · alumina + BN on a tetrahedral mesh (FEM)

presets.name: FEM · EMC stiffness and CTE on a tetrahedral mesh fitted to the particles
presets.description: Elasticity and thermal expansion solved by finite elements on a tetrahedral mesh fitted to the particles (Simulation → Solver settings → Elasticity and CTE → Finite elements on a tetrahedral mesh fitted to the particles), with the voxel finite elements (FANS) beside it ('Also solve with the other method'). Fused silica spheres (4 µm, log-normal) 60 vol% in epoxy, 16 µm RVE, 48³ voxels of 0.33 µm. Result (about 1 min): 1.63 million tetrahedra; 6,041 edges cross a film of resin between two spheres thinner than the mesh (median 0.19 µm), carried as interface elements. E 14.8 GPa and α 16.5 ppm/K by the FEM against E 21.7 GPa and α 11.8 ppm/K by the voxel elements on the same structure. The voxel value is not converged at this grid: two spheres are bonded wherever two of their voxels touch, and that stiff path thins as the grid is refined. The same recipe drawn on finer and finer grids (guide 12.2): voxel elements 24.8 → 21.8 → 20.1 → 18.2 → 17.2 → 16.2 GPa from 32³ to 192³ and still falling, the FEM 15.4 → 15.0 → 14.8 GPa from 32³ to 64³; α 10.3 → 15.6 ppm/K against 16.0 → 16.6. Extrapolated to an infinitely fine grid the two meet: 14.1-14.2 GPa and about 17 ppm/K. Against a measurement the FEM is the nearer one: glass spheres in epoxy at 23 to 50 vol% (Smith 1976; preset 'Measured benchmark') within −7 to +5 %, the voxel elements of the same grid 15 to 35 % high. Particles bonded over an area take a neck (Bonded contacts, guide 12.2). The Result Viewer shows the thermal stress in 3D on the mesh itself beside the voxel field. Interfaces are bonded (a cured compound at small strain). On the same mesh FEniCSx gives the same stiffness and thermal stress to twelve digits (self-test).

form.name: EMC · E and CTE on a tetrahedral mesh (FEM)

presets.name: FEM · grains with thin fibres on a graded tetrahedral mesh
presets.description: A blend of very different sizes on the graded mesh (Simulation → Solver settings → Tetrahedral mesh → Graded): irregular alumina grains (3 µm) 50 vol% with copper fibres 0.3 µm thick and 3 µm long, 1 vol%, in epoxy; 9 µm RVE, 60³ voxels of 0.15 µm - a fibre is two voxels thick. The graded mesh halves its cells where a particle's surface runs through them until they are a quarter of that particle's smallest dimension: 0.075 µm at the fibres (finer than the voxel), up to 0.6 µm inside the grains and in open resin; 3.70 million tetrahedra (about 1 min with the finite volume beside it). k_z 1.88 W/m·K by the FEM against 4.81 W/m·K by the finite volume on the voxels, which sees a fibre as a two-voxel staircase and conducts wherever two voxels touch. The 327 pairs that the packing left overlapping by less than a voxel are met as touching particles (Overlapping particles → Separated, the default since 5.12.0); merged into necks, as up to 5.11, they give 3.25. What the graded mesh saves depends on where the fine particles are (guide 7.2): grains with 0.6 vol% fibres 20 times thinner needed 3.6 times fewer tetrahedra than the lattice mesh of the same finest cell and 14 times fewer one level finer - a resolution the lattice mesh did not reach on a 16 GB computer; a dense blend whose fines fill the gaps between the coarse particles everywhere saved 15 to 30 %, since there the surfaces are everywhere.

form.name: Grains with thin fibres on a graded tetrahedral mesh (FEM)

presets.name: Measured benchmark · glass spheres 40 vol% in epoxy: FEM and voxel elements against 7.94 GPa

form.name: Glass spheres 40 vol% in epoxy · Smith 1976

presets.description: Which value is right? J. C. Smith (J. Res. Natl. Bur. Stand. A 80A (1976) 45, doi:10.6028/jres.080A.008, table 2) measured Young's modulus and Poisson's ratio of an epoxy filled with glass spheres of 1 to 30 µm, coated with an aminosilane, in tension at 24 °C: 7.94 ± 0.12 GPa and 0.354 at a volume fraction of 0.396 (unfilled 3.01 GPa, 0.394; glass 76 GPa, 0.23, as the paper states). This case is that compound - spheres of 10 µm (log-normal), 60 µm RVE, 48³ voxels - solved by the tetrahedral FEM with the voxel elements beside it. Result (about 1 min): E 8.15 GPa by the FEM (+2.6 % against the measurement), 10.68 GPa by the voxel elements on the same grid (+34.6 %). Over the paper's loadings 0.225 / 0.3025 / 0.396 / 0.496 the measurement is 5.08 / 6.01 / 7.94 / 12.09 GPa, the FEM 5.12 / 6.32 / 8.15 / 11.22 (+0.7 / +5.1 / +2.6 / -7.2 %), the voxel elements 5.82 / 7.62 / 10.68 / 16.16 at 48³ (+15 / +27 / +35 / +34 %), 5.36 / 6.79 / 9.09 / 13.14 at 96³ and 5.22 / 6.52 / 8.61 / 12.13 at 144³, still falling towards the FEM's. Spheres wetted by the resin meet at points with resin around them, which is the structure the FEM solves; the voxel elements bond every pair of touching voxels. At 0.496 the FEM is 7 % below the measurement (two seeds and equal spheres within 1 % of each other). Bonded contacts stay at 0 here.

presets.name: FEM · AlSiC, SiC 63 vol%: bonded contacts fitted to the measured expansion
presets.description: Particles that are bonded to each other. The baseplate preset (Al-Si7Mg + SiC 63 vol%, bimodal 60 + 20 µm) has a measured expansion of 8.21 ppm/K (Guo et al., J. Univ. Sci. Technol. Beijing 36 (2014) 489-495, doi:10.13374/j.issn1001-053x.2014.04.011). With the spheres as generated - touching at points, aluminium around them - the tetrahedral FEM gives 9.23 ppm/K: for these constituents the Hashin–Shtrikman bounds with Levin's relation allow 8.05 (the SiC a connected skeleton) to 9.51 ppm/K, and the measurement lies at the skeleton end. Simulation → Solver settings → Bonded contacts joins two particles where their surfaces come close - a neck of the radius entered (times the smaller particle's radius) where they touch, smaller where a gap is left: 9.23 / 9.15 / 8.86 / 8.20 ppm/K for 0 / 0.3 / 0.45 / 0.6. This case runs 0.6 on a 180 µm box (about 1 min): α 8.20 ppm/K and E 235 GPa with 782 pairs of particles joined, against 8.85 ppm/K and 222 GPa by the voxel elements, which bond wherever two voxels touch whatever is entered. The neck is fitted to this one measurement, not predicted: it stands for the contacts of an angular grit pressed together at 63 vol%, which spheres do not have. Use it that way - fit it to one measured value of a material and predict its other properties and loadings.

presets.name: Compression · silica 50 vol% with contacts and friction beside the resin flow

form.name: Compression with contacts and friction · silica 50 vol%

presets.description: What a dense compound resists a press with. Silica spheres of 5 µm at 50 vol% in an epoxy, a 25 µm RVE pressed by 30 % along z at 1 1/s with its sides free. The run solves the resin's flow on the voxels step by step (the compressed structure and its fields come from it), and presses the same spheres as rigid bodies by particle dynamics with lubrication films of their real width, contact springs and Coulomb friction (Domain → Particle arrangement → After compression → Contacts and friction; friction coefficient 0.25, roughness 5 nm: the contact inputs of Viscosity → particle dynamics). Result (about 1 min, resin 1 Pa·s at the equivalent shear rate): axial stress 14.4 Pa at the start and 80.2 Pa after 30 % with contacts and friction (26.7 times the plain resin's, 66 % of it carried by contacts, 2.9 contacts per sphere); 162 → 250 Pa by the flow on the voxels, where a film between two spheres is one voxel wide and nothing acts between sliding surfaces (a voxel half the size gave 2.4 times less). The same spheres reach 11.5, 25 and 35 times the plain resin's stress after 30 % for friction coefficients 0, 0.25 and 0.5; the shear viscosity of this suspension by the particle dynamics is 10.9, 23.9 and 35.2 times the resin's. The stress starts low because a generated packing has no contacts yet and builds them as it is pressed. Spheres in one resin without pores or cure, a side free.

presets.name: Benchmark · Rayleigh's simple cubic array of spheres (conduction)

form.name: Benchmark · Rayleigh's simple cubic array of spheres

presets.description: A literature solution reproduced. One sphere in a periodic cube is a simple cubic array of spheres, the problem Lord Rayleigh solved (Philos. Mag. 34 (1892) 481, doi:10.1080/14786449208620364): spheres of 4 µm in cells of 6 µm (15.5 vol%), 100 times as conducting as the matrix. Rayleigh's series with the coefficient of its φ^(10/3) term as later corrected, 0.525, gives k/k_m = 1.5324; with Rayleigh's printed 1.65, 1.5338. Result (seconds, 48³): 1.5347 by the FEM on the mesh fitted to the sphere (+0.15 %), 1.5394 by the finite volume on voxels (+0.46 %). The FEM converges with the square of the voxel size (self-test: 1.5655, 1.5428, 1.5361, 1.5342 with the sphere 5, 11, 21, 32 voxels across). Domain → Periodic array is on: the box is one cell of the array, so the RVE-size and particle-count criteria of a random RVE are shown as not applicable.

presets.name: Benchmark · Hasselman–Johnson: dilute spheres with an interfacial resistance

form.name: Benchmark · Hasselman–Johnson: spheres with an interfacial resistance

presets.description: A literature solution reproduced. Spheres of 4 µm, 20 times as conducting as the matrix, at 5 vol% (one sphere per periodic cell), with an interfacial thermal resistance R on their surface. D. P. H. Hasselman and L. F. Johnson (J. Compos. Mater. 21 (1987) 508, doi:10.1177/002199838702100602) give the conductivity of dilute spheres with an interface of conductance 1/R through α = R k_m / a (a the radius). The preset is a DOE over R = 0, 1e-6 and 2e-6 m²K/W (α 0, 0.5, 1); it opens in the DOE tab. Result (seconds per case, 70³): α 0: 1.1357 against 1.1355 (+0.02 %); α 0.5: 1.0326 against 1.0325 (+0.01 %); α 1: 0.9977 against 0.9976 (+0.01 %). At α = 1 the sphere is nearly invisible, k ≈ k_m. The resistance sits on the sphere's own surface on the tetrahedral mesh (the thermal conductivity's default since 5.12.0; on the voxel faces with the finite volume, scaled by the ratio of the sphere's area to that of its staircase: 1.1363 / 1.0311 / 0.9960). Domain → Periodic array is on.

presets.name: Benchmark · Maxwell Garnett: permittivity of dilute spheres

form.name: Benchmark · Maxwell Garnett: dilute dielectric spheres

presets.description: A literature solution reproduced. Spheres of permittivity 100 (a BaTiO3-like filler) in a matrix of 3 at 5 vol%, one sphere per periodic cell. J. C. Maxwell Garnett (Philos. Trans. R. Soc. Lond. A 203 (1904) 385, doi:10.1098/rsta.1904.0024) gives the permittivity of dilute spheres: 3.4320 at the drawn content. Result (seconds, 70³): 3.4355 (+0.10 %). At 5 vol% the array and the dilute limit differ by less than this. Domain → Periodic array is on.

presets.name: Benchmark · Einstein: viscosity of a dilute rigid sphere

form.name: Benchmark · Einstein: a dilute rigid sphere in a viscous resin

presets.description: A literature solution reproduced. One rigid sphere of 4 µm in a periodic cube of 12 µm (1.9 vol%) in a Newtonian resin, sheared: the voxel flow solve of the viscosity analysis (particle dynamics off). A. Einstein (Ann. Phys. 324 (1906) 289, doi:10.1002/andp.19063240204, with the correction of Ann. Phys. 339 (1911) 591, doi:10.1002/andp.19113390313) gives 1 + 2.5 φ for dilute rigid spheres: 1.0485. Result (about 1 min, 120³, the sphere 40 voxels across): 1.0501, an intrinsic viscosity [η] = 2.59 (+3.44 %): the voxelised sphere and its periodic images add a few per cent at this content. Domain → Periodic array is on.

presets.name: Benchmark · Trouton: compression of a resin alone

form.name: Benchmark · Trouton: compression of a resin alone

presets.description: A literature solution reproduced. A box of resin without filler pressed by 10 % along z at 1 1/s, its sides free: the flow solve of the compression (Domain → Particle arrangement → After compression). F. T. Trouton (Proc. R. Soc. Lond. A 77 (1906) 426, doi:10.1098/rspa.1906.0038) showed that a viscous liquid resists uniaxial extension or compression with three times its shear viscosity: σ_zz = −3 η ε̇ = -3 Pa for η = 1 Pa·s. Result (seconds): -3 Pa at every step. With one side held (plane strain) the factor is 4 (self-test).

presets.name: Benchmark · two layers: series and parallel (exact)

form.name: Benchmark · two layers: series and parallel

presets.description: An exact solution reproduced, from an image (Structure → Load TIFF; the image ships with MPSim): a cube of 32³ voxels of 1 µm, the lower half epoxy (k 0.2 W/m·K, ε_r 3.9), the upper half alumina (k 30, ε_r 9.8). Across the layers the two conduct in series, k = 2/(1/k1 + 1/k2) = 0.39735 W/m·K; along them in parallel, (k1 + k2)/2 = 15.1; the same for the permittivity, 5.57956 and 6.85. Result (seconds): k_z 0.39735, k_x 15.1; ε_z 5.57956, ε_x 6.85 - the exact values. These are the Wiener bounds, which every run checks its result against. Domain → Periodic array is on.

presets.name: Benchmark · Poiseuille: a straight cylindrical pore (flow, tortuosity, acoustic lengths)

form.name: Benchmark · Poiseuille: a straight cylindrical pore

presets.description: Exact solutions reproduced, from an image (it ships with MPSim): a straight cylindrical pore of radius 16 µm along x through a solid, in a cell of 32 × 80 × 80 voxels of 1 µm (porosity 12.7 %). Laminar flow through a straight tube (Hagen–Poiseuille) gives the permeability K = φ r²/8 = 4.060e-12 m² for the flow along the pore; the pore is straight, so the tortuosity is 1; and the viscous and thermal characteristic lengths of D. L. Johnson, J. Koplik and R. Dashen (J. Fluid Mech. 176 (1987) 379, doi:10.1017/S0022112087000727) both equal the radius for straight pores. Result (seconds): K 3.914e-12 m² (-3.60 %: the circle drawn on voxels is a staircase, which adds drag), τ 1.0000, Λ 15.85 µm and Λ′ 15.85 µm. Domain → Periodic array is on.

presets.name: Benchmark · Maxwell: moisture diffusion around impermeable spheres

form.name: Benchmark · Maxwell: moisture around impermeable spheres

presets.description: A literature solution reproduced. Silica spheres of 4 µm, which take up no water, at 5 vol% in epoxy (one sphere per periodic cell): the moisture analysis. For impermeable spheres J. C. Maxwell's solution (A Treatise on Electricity and Magnetism, Vol. 1, Clarendon Press, Oxford, 1873, §314; a book without DOI) gives the diffusivity of the compound per concentration in the resin, D*/D_m = 2/(2 + φ) = 0.9756. Result (seconds, 70³): 0.9726 (-0.31 %). The uptake curve of the plate is Crank's series solution, which the self-test checks to 2e-3 (half saturation at 0.04919 L²/D). Domain → Periodic array is on.

presets.name: Benchmark · DOE · glass spheres in epoxy at Smith's four loadings: FEM and voxel elements against the measurement

form.name: Glass spheres in epoxy · Smith 1976, four loadings

presets.description: Which value is right, against a published measurement. J. C. Smith (J. Res. Natl. Bur. Stand. A 80A (1976) 45, doi:10.6028/jres.080A.008, table 2) measured Young's modulus and Poisson's ratio of an epoxy (3.01 GPa, ν 0.394) filled with glass spheres of 1 to 30 µm coated with an aminosilane (76 GPa, ν 0.23), in tension at 24 °C, 200 days after casting. This DOE runs the paper's four loadings with the tetrahedral FEM and the voxel elements on the same particles (spheres of 10 µm, log-normal; 60 µm RVE, 48³). Result (about 1 min per case): 22.51 vol%: measured 5.08 ± 0.08 GPa, FEM 5.12 (+0.70 %), voxel elements 5.83 (+14.71 %); 30.25 vol%: measured 6.01 ± 0.21 GPa, FEM 6.32 (+5.08 %), voxel elements 7.62 (+26.75 %); 39.6 vol%: measured 7.94 ± 0.12 GPa, FEM 8.15 (+2.63 %), voxel elements 10.68 (+34.57 %); 49.6 vol%: measured 12.09 ± 0.09 GPa, FEM 11.22 (-7.22 %), voxel elements 16.16 (+33.68 %). Poisson's ratio: measured 0.384 / 0.375 / 0.354 / 0.330, FEM 0.365 / 0.352 / 0.336 / 0.314. The voxel elements bond every pair of touching voxels; on finer grids they fall towards the FEM (at 39.6 vol%: 10.68 / 9.09 / 8.61 GPa at 48³ / 96³ / 144³). Two criteria fail by design at this grid: the spheres are 4.7 voxels across and the box 3 times the largest sphere - what the comparison is about; a second packing moved the FEM by 1 %, equal spheres by 1 %, a 64³ mesh by 2 %.

presets.name: Sensitivity · alumina in epoxy: which of content, particle size and the two conductivities moves k (DOE, 24 cases)
presets.description: The example of the Sensitivity Analysis tab. Four inputs of an alumina-filled epoxy are varied together over a 24-case Latin hypercube - the alumina content (20-50 vol%), the particle diameter (6-14 µm), the filler's and the matrix's conductivity - and the thermal conductivity of every case is computed (60 µm RVE, 48³ voxels; the thermal conductivity on the tetrahedral FEM, about 34 s per case, 13 min for the study one case after another). Create the study on the DOE tab, then open Sensitivity Analysis, choose Thermal conductivity and press Analyse. Result (MPSim 5.12.0, guide chapter 28A): the content leads in all 25 measures and takes part in 62 % of the variance (Sobol S_T on a Gaussian process, cross-validated Q² 0.98); the matrix conductivity follows (consensus 0.73, S_T 0.39), then the diameter (0.17) and the filler's conductivity (0.14, S_T 0.02): with a filler 14-230 times the resin, the heat crosses the resin films between the particles, so the resin's conductivity counts and the filler's hardly. Content × matrix conductivity is the one interaction three of five measures find (PCE S₂ 0.014, ANOVA p = 1.3e-6): the resin's conductivity matters more at a high loading. Interactions carry 3 % of the variance; the 25 measures agree with Kendall's W = 0.88. (On the voxels, MPSim 5.11 found the filler's conductivity weighing more: consensus 0.25 against the matrix's 0.44.) The realised contents and diameters of the generated structures are the inputs (they differ from the targets by up to a few per cent).

presets.name: Benchmark · particle dynamics against Krieger–Dougherty (frictionless spheres, 50 vol%)

form.name: Benchmark · particle dynamics against Krieger–Dougherty (frictionless spheres, 50 vol%)

presets.description: A published model reproduced by the particle dynamics of the viscosity analysis. 500 spheres of 10 µm (the particle dynamics draws them with a CV of 0.1: equal spheres order into sliding layers) at 50 vol% in a Newtonian liquid of 1 Pa·s, sheared at 10 1/s to a strain of 10 (the mean over the second half): lubrication between close surfaces with a roughness of 5 nm, contact springs, no attraction. Without friction the spheres jam at random close packing, and I. M. Krieger and T. J. Dougherty (Trans. Soc. Rheol. 3 (1959) 137, doi:10.1122/1.548848) with φm 0.64 and [η] 2.5 gives 11.38. Result (about 4 min): 11.77 ± 0.61 (+3.46 %). At 40 and 55 vol% the same runs gave 5.70 and 18.55 against 4.80 and 23.07: the frictionless suspension follows the law at 50 vol% and departs from it as it approaches jamming, where Krieger-Dougherty is an empirical fit rather than a solution.

presets.name: Benchmark · particle dynamics against Boyer et al.'s measured law (friction 0.25, 50 vol%)

form.name: Benchmark · particle dynamics against Boyer et al.'s measured law (friction 0.25, 50 vol%)

presets.description: Against a published measurement. 500 spheres of 10 µm (the particle dynamics draws them with a CV of 0.1: equal spheres order into sliding layers) at 50 vol% in a Newtonian liquid of 1 Pa·s, sheared at 10 1/s to a strain of 10 (the mean over the second half): lubrication between close surfaces with a roughness of 5 nm, contact springs, no attraction. Friction coefficient 0.25 (the default). F. Boyer, É. Guazzelli and O. Pouliquen (Phys. Rev. Lett. 107 (2011) 188301, doi:10.1103/PhysRevLett.107.188301) measured non-Brownian spheres in a viscous liquid under imposed pressure and gave the shear viscosity as eq. (8), with μ1 0.32, μ2 0.7, I0 0.005 and φm 0.585: 31.9 at 50 vol%. Result (about 5 min): 22.9 ± 1.2 (-28.29 %). At 40 / 55 vol% the law gives 7.39 / 145, the particle dynamics 6.09 / 104 with friction 0.25 and 6.45 / 409 with 0.5 (30.3 at 50 vol%): no single coefficient follows the law over the three loadings. Earlier versions gave this law as 20.7 at 50 vol% and chose 0.25 with it - an evaluation without the (μ2 − μ1) part of the contact term.
